newsitem.title: USA: Ocampo sees Colombia GDP growing 4 pct in 97 -- RFTV.
newsitem.headline: Ocampo sees Colombia GDP growing 4 pct in 97 -- RFTV.

text.p: Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said on Tuesday he was confident that Colombia's gross domestic product would grow by around four percent in 1997, up from last year's 2.1 percent increase.
"I think a four percent target, which is really a joint target we have with the Central Bank, is acceptable," he said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

"In fact, major analysts in Colombia like Fedesarrollo, the major think tanks, are keeping a four percent projection for the year. Other analysts are a bit lower than that, but we are fairly confident about four percent," he added.
Ocampo said the recovery would be fuelled by higher demand, thanks to a decline in domestic interest rates and a rise in coffee prices that started late last year.
Colombia kept interest rates high between late 1994 and early 1996 to cool down its economy and reduce inflation, which had remained hovering stubbornly above 20 percent.
Its economy was also affected by an unexpected drop in the coffee crop between late 1996 and early 1997 and the rising cost of waging war against drug traffickers, Ocampo argued.
Ocampo added that he remained "fairly confident" that Colombian interest rates would continue to decrease.
The central bank's board will meet on May 6 to review its rate policy in the light of April's inflation results.
Last week Ocampo, who sits on the board, proposed that the central bank cut its overnight rate by two percentage points to 19.5 percent.
"I'm fairly confident that there will be some reduction in interest rates," he said."Whether the board will go for my two (percentage) points reduction proposal, I still don't know."
"In any case, there is a fairly general consensus among the board that we should bring down nominal interest rates as inflation comes down," Ocampo added.
Regarding a brewing controversy over the health of Colombia' savings and loan industry, Ocampo stated that he did not think the sector was in any danger at all.
"Actually, the bad loans of the S&L industry are among the lowest in the Colombian financial system, which are, again, low by international standards," he said.
The decline in interest rates and the economic recovery, coupled with some measures to refinance non-performing loans, should help both indebted households and S&Ls, Ocampo said.
"I think this is more of a political phenomenon than an economic one," he added, alluding to a fledgling debtor protest movement in Colombia.

Ocampo said the S&L measures would have no significant fiscal impact, adding that the improvement in coffee prices would produce a larger than expected surplus in the National Coffee Fund, allowing Colombia to keep its overall fiscal deficit at close to one percent of GDP.
Colombia resorted to emergency fiscal measures early this year to close a yawning fiscal gap but those policies were voided by a constitutional court.
In an effort to improve revenue, the government of President Ernesto Samper last week sent the Colombian congress a tax reform proposal focusing on fighting tax evasion.

Ocampo added that he was working with Colombia's National Planning Office on a major cut in the public sector's investment budget in order to postpone outlays until 1998. The reduction would be announced in the next few weeks, he said.
-- Peter Bate, IMF newsroom (( 202 898 8377))
